"Workplace culture" ( V-0006 ) is a concept many learners over-translate word-for-word, which can make it sound distant or academic in Bengali. It's simpler than it sounds: it just means the shared, mostly unwritten habits of how people treat each other at a particular workplace — something you notice within your first few weeks, not something you need to memorize a definition for.

Bengali doesn't require a separate verb form for "still true now" versus "finished in the past" the way English's present perfect does, so it's easy to default to simple past or simple present for both. A quick test: if the sentence is still true or relevant right now (a skill you still have, an interest you still hold), reach for present perfect ("I've been interested in..."); if it's simply a completed fact, past simple ("I studied...") is enough.

Present perfect ("I've finished") signals a completed action with present relevance — exactly what "done" needs. Present continuous ("I'm working on") signals something happening right now — exactly what "doing" needs. Bengali and Hindi speakers often use a simple past form where English prefers the present perfect, so they say "I finished the checklist" when "I've finished the checklist" fits a status update better: the finished task still matters to what happens next, which is exactly what the present perfect signals. ("I just finished…" is also common, especially in American English.)
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: Bengali and Hindi often relay a message by directly quoting the original speaker's words, sometimes without shifting tense or pronouns, and letting context and tone carry the meaning. In English, the pronoun shift (and, after a past reporting verb, often a tense shift) is what tells the listener this is now your description of the exchange, not a direct quote. Learning to make that shift deliberately, rather than skipping it, is what makes a relayed message sound natural in English.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: In Bengali and Hindi workplace messaging, the shift between a formal written register and a casual spoken one is often marked mainly by vocabulary choice and honorifics, with sentence structure staying fairly similar across both. English chat register shifts more structurally — whole words and connecting phrases get dropped, not just swapped for casual synonyms. Recognizing this as a structural shift, not just a "casual word choice" shift, helps explain why a direct translation from a formal Bengali/Hindi message often reads as overly formal in English chat.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: In some Bengali and Hindi workplace contexts, repeating "sorry" too many times can actually read as insincere or overly dramatic, and a brief, sincere acknowledgment is preferred over an extended apology. In English professional contexts, the opposite risk is more common — a single quick "sorry" can read as dismissive precisely because it's so brief. The fix in English isn't saying "sorry" more times — it's adding the ownership and prevention steps that make one sincere "sorry" feel complete.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: In Bengali and Hindi, honorifics and respectful forms of address (such as "Sir/Madam," "Apu," "Bhaiya," or a title before a name) are woven into the grammar and everyday speech far more consistently than in English, where respect is shown mainly through title-plus-surname and tone rather than through the language's own structure. English learners sometimes under-signal respect in English for exactly this reason — not because they intend to be casual, but because English simply doesn't offer as many automatic honorific markers, so the respect has to be built deliberately into word choice and phrasing instead.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: Traditional Bengali and Hindi formal letters often open with an elaborate, respectful greeting line before the actual subject is mentioned at all. In English business email, that same instinct can backfire — a long, formal opening before the point is made often reads as less professional, not more, because it delays information the reader needs immediately. English professional email greetings are deliberately short ("Hi," "Dear," plus a name) precisely so the email can get to its purpose in the very next line. Respect is shown through clarity and a courteous closing, not through an elaborate opening.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: In everyday Bengali and Hindi reporting — telling a colleague or a family member what happened — it is completely natural, even expected, to blend what happened with what you think about it in the very same sentence: "The kitchen was so disorganized, the guest was obviously furious." English professional reporting convention asks you to separate these two things deliberately, not because feeling and judgment don't matter, but because a report is meant to be checkable by someone who wasn't there. Save your judgment for the Analysis and Recommendation sections, where it's not only allowed but expected.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Bengali/Hindi note: In many Bengali and Hindi conversational norms, responding quickly while someone is speaking — a quick "hmm," a nod, an early word of agreement — signals attentiveness and respect. In English professional listening, the same instinct can come across as interrupting. The fix isn't to seem less engaged — it's to hold your response until the customer has genuinely finished, and then show you were listening the whole time through what you reflect back, not through how quickly you responded.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: in Bengali and Hindi professional custom, a warm, even elaborate welcome for a visiting guest is often expected and can run quite long before business begins — hospitality itself is the message. In English client-facing contexts internationally, the warmth is still expected, but it is usually compressed into one or two genuine lines before moving to purpose; a client who is kept in extended welcome-talk may start to read it as stalling rather than as respect.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: in many Bengali and Hindi professional contexts, a guest or client is sometimes shown respect by not being questioned too directly — the host is expected to anticipate needs rather than ask about them. In English client-facing contexts, the opposite is often true: asking thoughtful, specific questions is read as attentiveness and professionalism, not as a lack of preparation.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: in Bengali and Hindi business custom, presenting many options generously — even beyond what was asked — can be a way of showing hospitality and effort. In English client-facing contexts, presenting fewer options, each explicitly tied to a stated need, usually reads as more attentive and more professional than presenting many options at once, which can come across as not having listened closely enough to narrow things down.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: in Bengali and Hindi business custom, price is very often negotiated openly and immediately, and a quick concession can be read as generosity and goodwill. In many international client-facing contexts, an immediate, unqualified discount can instead read as a sign the original price wasn't honest in the first place. A calm, honest explanation plus one specific, deliverable reassurance usually builds more trust than an instant price cut.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Bengali/Hindi note: Bengali and Hindi grammar don't use articles the way English does, so this is often the single most persistent accuracy gap for Bengali- and Hindi-speaking writers — not a small detail, but a genuinely different grammatical habit to build. It's worth naming plainly rather than glossing over: expect this to take real, repeated practice, and expect to still miss a few articles even at an advanced level. That's normal, and it rarely affects whether the reader understands you.

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: Bengali and Hindi both distribute emphasis across a word's syllables more evenly than English does — English is unusually dependent on one strong, clearly marked stressed syllable per word. This is a genuine, persistent difference, not a small one, and it's one of the main reasons multi-syllable English words can feel unpredictable at first. The fix isn't to imitate a particular accent — it's to learn the stress pattern of each new professional word the same way you'd learn its spelling: as a fixed fact about that specific word.

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: in Bengali and Hindi hospitality and workplace custom, refusing a loyal or senior person directly can feel unusually blunt, and there is often real social pressure to find some way to say yes, even partially. In many international professional contexts, a firm, respectfully repeated "no" is read as more trustworthy than a "no" that visibly bends under a second request — because it shows the same rule applies to everyone. Holding the line calmly is not disrespect; it is what makes the respect shown to the next guest, colleague, or client mean something.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: in Bengali and Hindi workplace custom, direct criticism — especially between peers of similar standing — can feel unusually blunt, and it is common to soften a critical point heavily or avoid it altogether to protect the relationship. In many professional contexts internationally, staying silent about a real, repeated problem is read as a bigger risk to the relationship than raising it clearly and specifically, because the problem itself keeps costing the other person unnoticed. Naming the behavior specifically — never the character — is what keeps the criticism safe to hear.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: correcting someone's work directly, including a senior correcting a junior, can carry more weight and formality in Bengali and Hindi professional custom than the words alone suggest — and the instinct to explain oneself immediately, to preserve standing, can be strong. In many professional contexts internationally, a quick, genuine "that's fair" before any explanation is read as more confident, not less — it signals the person is secure enough to hear a correction without needing to win the exchange first.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: raising a pattern of dismissiveness with a peer directly can feel confrontational in Bengali and Hindi workplace custom, where such friction is often absorbed quietly or raised indirectly through a third party instead. In many professional contexts internationally, addressing it directly but calmly — without an audience, without heat, framed as solving a shared problem — is seen as the healthier and more respectful choice, both for the relationship and for the work that keeps getting affected by it.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: this is one of the more important distinctions in this module, so it's worth stating plainly. Presenting the same true fact from a favorable, purposeful angle is a normal and honest part of professional persuasion in both Bengali/Hindi and English-language workplaces. It becomes spin the moment a fact that would change the listener's decision is hidden or softened past recognition — and once a listener catches that once, they tend to re-check everything else you tell them afterward. The line isn't about which language you're arguing in; it's whether the argument would still hold up if the listener knew everything you chose not to say.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: in Bengali and Hindi professional custom, presenting to a senior figure often involves a longer, deferential lead-in before reaching the main point, as a mark of respect for hierarchy. In executive English communication internationally, the opposite convention usually applies: leading with the conclusion is read as a sign of respect for the senior person's time, not as bluntness. A learner moving between these two conventions should read "bottom line first" as a different, equally respectful way of honoring a senior listener's attention, not as skipping a courtesy.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: Bengali and Hindi professional communication, especially when speaking with someone senior, often leans toward the high-context, hierarchy-aware end of these same dimensions — a flat "no" to a senior person is frequently softened into an indirect phrase, and a pause before answering can itself be doing communicative work, exactly like the guest's pause at checkout in this lesson. This isn't vagueness; it's a coherent, high-context style, sitting at a real point on the very dimensions taught here. A Bengali- or Hindi-influenced speaker moving into a more low-context, direct workplace often needs to consciously add explicitness that their own instinct reads as slightly blunt — and the reverse is just as true for someone moving the other way, into a Bengali- or Hindi-majority workplace, from a more direct starting style.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Bengali/Hindi note: in Bengali and Hindi business custom, raising a vendor's failures too directly can feel like a personal accusation against the account manager, even when the fault lies with their company's systems — there can be pressure to soften the message until it barely names the problem. In many international vendor-management contexts, naming the specific pattern with evidence and a date is read as businesslike and fair, not personal, precisely because it treats the vendor as capable of fixing it rather than simply at fault.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

In Bengali and Hindi workplace custom, a person recently promoted often continues speaking deferentially toward their own team for some time, out of humility and respect for colleagues who may be older or more experienced. This instinct is a good one and should not disappear — but it should not be confused with hedging a decision that is now genuinely the speaker's to make. "As I see it" and "my call on this is" can be said warmly and respectfully; they simply state the judgment plainly instead of disguising it as a question. Respect for the team and clarity about who now owns the decision are not in conflict.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: Many Bengali- and Hindi-speaking learners are taught, quite reasonably, that modesty is a mark of good character — that a person shouldn't be the one to list their own accomplishments. An English-language CV works on a different, opposite assumption: nobody else is going to describe your achievements for you, so if you don't state them clearly and specifically, the reader simply never learns about them. This isn't the same as boasting. A CV that says "achieved a 95% satisfaction score" is stating a fact, the same way a report states a fact — it is expected, professional, and necessary in this context, not immodest. The discomfort of writing this way is normal at first; the skill is learning to state real achievements plainly, without either hiding them or exaggerating them.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)

Original Text: For some Bengali- and Hindi-speaking learners, raised in workplace cultures where recognition is expected to come from a supervisor noticing your work rather than from asking for it directly, proactively requesting feedback or raising a promotion can feel forward, even slightly uncomfortable — as though you're claiming credit that should be given, not asked for. In many English-speaking professional cultures, the opposite is closer to true: initiating these conversations is a normal, expected professional move, not an overstep. A supervisor is often genuinely glad an employee raised it, because it removes the guesswork of when to bring it up themselves. Learning to ask, calmly and with evidence, is a skill — not a breach of respect.
Review Required: Native Bengali and Hindi speakers (check the claim)
